Why does my video suck?

Read the picture. It tells you where to look.

▶  Present the slides

Every FPV pilot has had a bad picture: snow, lines, a black screen, somebody else's view in their goggles. The good news is that the picture itself tells you what is wrong. Each kind of bad picture points at a different part of the system. Learn to read it, and you stop guessing.

The video chain

Your picture travels along a chain. The camera sees the track. The video transmitter (VTX) turns that into a radio signal, and the antenna on the drone sends it into the air. On the other side, the antenna on your goggles catches it, the goggles turn it back into a picture, and finally your own eyes have to see it clearly. If any link breaks, the picture gets worse. Half of that chain sits on your head, so before you blame the drone, rule out the goggles.

Read the picture

  • Snow: the signal is weak. Look at the antennas, the distance, and what is in the way.
  • Lines that follow the throttle: electrical noise from the motors and ESCs.
  • Someone else in your picture, or bars rolling through it: another pilot on or next to your channel.
  • Black and white, or a picture that rolls: the camera and the goggles are set to different video standards (PAL and NTSC).
  • Black, but the OSD numbers still show: the camera or its cable. The VTX is working, because the numbers come through it.
  • Clean, but blurry: this isn't the signal at all. It's the lens, fog, or the focus of your goggles.

Snow: the signal is weak

Check the antennas first. Most snow comes from an antenna that is broken, loose or wrong, either on the drone or on your goggles. FPV antennas are circularly polarised, either right-hand (RHCP) or left-hand (LHCP), and both ends must be the same. Mix them and you lose most of your signal. You usually can't tell them apart by looking, so check the label. An antenna with a cracked tip or a loose connector can look fine and still fly badly. And never power up a drone without its antenna: the VTX has nowhere to send its power and can burn out.

Then look at what is between you and the drone. At 5.8 GHz the signal doesn't go through much: bodies, walls, reinforced concrete and trees all block it. Flying behind something, or far away, gives you snow.

At HOBIzone we never fix snow with more power. Our rule is 25 mW, always, in practice and in races. Fix the antennas instead.

The noise floor

Snow doesn't always mean your signal is weak. It can also mean everything else is loud. Your receiver hears every signal on its band, and your own signal has to stand out above all of it. That background level is called the noise floor.

Some of the noise is right next to you: WiFi, Bluetooth, phones, DJI goggles and air units, and other pilots' video. Some comes from further away: power lines, cell towers and radar. These are strong, they are not always clean, and they don't always stay inside their own band.

Indoors it gets messier. In a hall every signal bounces off the walls, the floor and the ceiling, yours and everybody else's. The echoes arrive a moment later than the direct signal and mix in with it: in analog video that looks like ghosting, tearing or sudden breakups in one part of the room. Circularly polarised antennas reject part of the echoes, because a single reflection flips the polarisation. But only part: a shallow bounce, or a signal that bounced twice, still gets through. And a bigger, more sensitive antenna isn't always the answer. It hears more of the noise as well as more of your signal. With lots of interference, small antennas, or sometimes no antennas at all on the goggles, can give a cleaner picture than big sensitive ones.

A higher noise floor means less room for your signal. You get snow sooner, your range is shorter, and the radio control link fails earlier too, because it has to be heard above the same noise. ExpressLRS shows it on the screen: the link quality drops long before the signal strength gets anywhere near its limit.

The good news: noise is often only on part of the band. 5 GHz WiFi, for example, sits on top of some FPV channels and not others. So when a spot or a channel is always bad, try another channel. A handy tool is a spectrum analyser, which shows the whole band at once, so you can see where the noise is. Make sure it covers 5.8 GHz. They have got cheap: a small ESP32-C5 board plugged into an Android phone with the free ESPsoup app scans the band, and it can even show analog FPV video. Some receiver modules also have a simple band scan. And look around: move away from the source, switch off what you don't need near the pits, and keep your antennas in good shape.

Not just noise: other interference

The noise floor is the background. On top of it, a few kinds of interference come up again and again, and each one has its own fix.

  • Same or next channel. Another pilot is too close to you in frequency. You see a ghost image or rolling bars. Spread out on the channel plan (more on the next slides).
  • Mixing (IMD). Two transmitters close together mix and create a third frequency, and it can land right on someone else's channel. Evenly spaced channels make it worse, which is why a good channel plan is deliberately uneven (see the Kollane field code).
  • Overload. A very strong transmitter right next to your goggles, like a drone powered up in the pits, can deafen your receiver even when it's on a different channel. The receiver gets less sensitive to everything. That's one more reason for the pit rules.
  • Dirty transmitters. A VTX doesn't always stay inside its own channel. A cheap, damaged or overheated one can leak energy onto the channels next to it and hurt the neighbours. Where the wires go matters too. On an HDZero Race V3, for example, a camera (MIPI) or antenna cable lying across the RF amplifier next to the antenna plug makes the VTX spray noise over almost three channels. Your own picture can stay perfect while the pilots next to you get the noise.
  • Antenna tuning. Every antenna is tuned to a centre frequency and works best near it. A bent or damaged antenna, or a cheap one, can drift off, so some channels work worse than others. An SWR meter shows how well an antenna is tuned across the band.
  • Dead spots. Indoors, an echo can arrive exactly out of step with the direct signal and cancel it. You get a spot where the picture always breaks up. Move a metre and it comes back.

Lines that follow the throttle

If thin lines run across the picture and get worse every time you punch out, it isn't the radio, it's electricity. Motors and ESCs make electrical noise, and it travels through the wires into the camera and the VTX. Watch your DVR: if the lines come and go with the throttle, it's noise.

The usual fix is a low-ESR capacitor soldered across the main battery pads, with legs as short as possible: around 470 µF on a small build and up to 1000 µF on a 5″, rated above the voltage of your fully charged battery. Wiring helps too: camera and VTX on the same ground, and powered from the flight controller's filtered pads (often marked 5V or 9V for the VTX), not from unfiltered pads or straight from the battery. Keep the VTX itself and its wires away from the noisy parts: the ESC, the motor wires and the battery leads. When you test on the bench: props off, always.

Was it someone else?

If your picture was fine and then suddenly wasn't, look around before you look at your drone. A ghost image, bars rolling through the picture, or somebody else's view in your goggles means two video signals are too close in frequency. Maybe someone just plugged in on your channel, or did a "quick test" in the pits. Maybe two pilots are on channels right next to each other. Ask "who just plugged in?", check the channel screen, and spread out across raceband.

It's not always the drone

Your goggles have antennas too, often two, and they need the same checks as the drone: not bent, not loose, the same polarisation. Your head is also in the way. If you turn your back on the drone, your own head blocks the signal and the picture breaks up, so face the track.

And keep your head up. Many pilots drop their chin low without noticing, and that aims the antennas the wrong way. A patch antenna on the front of the goggles then points at your feet instead of the drone. An omni (the stick on top) sends and receives out to the sides but almost nothing off its tip, and with your chin down, that blind tip points towards the drone. It looks like you are trying to ruin your own picture, but most people don't realise they're doing it.

If the picture is clean but blurry, it isn't the signal. Set the focus and the eye distance (IPD) on your goggles, wipe the camera lens, and give the goggles a moment to clear if they fog up when you come into a warm hall from the cold. If the picture is grey or keeps rolling, check that the camera and the goggles are set to the same standard, PAL or NTSC.

Find it like a detective

Good troubleshooting is a habit. Change one thing at a time, and test after every change.

  1. What kind of bad? Snow, lines, ghost, grey, black or blurry.
  2. Drone or goggles? Try a friend's goggles on your channel, or your goggles on a friend's drone. Now you know which half is broken.
  3. Antennas, both ends. Tight, straight, the same polarisation.
  4. Settings. Band, channel, 25 mW, pit mode off, PAL or NTSC.
  5. Wires and parts. The camera cable, solder joints, the capacitor. Swap one part, and test again.

You don't need perfect video

Race video is rarely clean. There are four drones in the air, a hall full of walls and people, and a rival right next to you. The best pilots fly through the static. Fix what you can before the race, keep flying during the heat, and afterwards check your DVR and fix the next thing.

We fly frying pans: nobody else is cooking. Bad video is something you can make better, not somebody else's fault.

Read the picture. It tells you where to look.
